**Effects of Nested Navigation Patterns on Item-Finding Speed and Error Recovery**

| Gerylyn Guiller | Qinpei Lu | Naomi Reyes | Lyrshe Weng |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |

**ABSTRACT**

Government websites provide diverse audiences access to numerous services through nested menus, yet the effects of different navigation designs on task completion and error recovery remain unclear. This study proposes a three-phase investigation of navigation patterns on Philippine government websites. First, existing navigation patterns will be documented, and a reference website will be selected. Second, three low-fidelity prototypes of the reference site will be developed, featuring automated timers and event logging. Third, an in-person, within-subjects usability test will be conducted using researcher-provided phones. The study will compare three navigation styles: deep hierarchical menus, mega-menus, and nested dropdowns. Their usability will be evaluated on item-finding time, navigation errors, and recovery time. By examining both task efficiency and error recovery, this research aims to provide insights into navigation design for government websites. This paper presents the research questions, measurement methods, testing procedures, and analysis plan, establishing the future data collection.

**CCS CONCEPTS**

• Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in HCI; Usability testing; Web-based interaction.

**KEYWORDS**

navigation design, hierarchical menus, mega-menus, government websites, Philippines, usability testing, item-finding time

# **1  Introduction**

Government websites are how many people renew documents, claim benefits, pay taxes, and look up regulations. A single national portal may expose hundreds or thousands of pages to citizens, businesses, and visitors, so its navigation is almost always organized as a nested hierarchy. Visitors typically arrive with a concrete goal, such as finding one particular form or service page, and navigation is the main route to it.

Designers have several ways to present that hierarchy. Users may drill down through many narrow levels of a deep hierarchy, open a large panel that shows many sub-levels at once (a mega-menu), or expand cascading dropdowns. Nielsen Norman Group reports suggest these choices matter: hiding navigation reduces discoverability and slows task completion \[4\], and a usability study of the USA.gov mega-menus found problems with images and topic labels even though overall task success was good \[3\]. What remains unclear is how these nested styles compare with one another for the same kind of goal, finding a specific item on a government website. This study examines that question for Philippine government websites.

The problem is difficult for three reasons. First, navigation performance depends on the interplay of visibility, breadth, depth, and labeling, so styles are hard to compare in isolation. Live sites rarely change one of these factors without changing the others, so differences in speed cannot be cleanly attributed to the navigation style itself. Second, there is no settled inventory of which nested patterns Philippine government sites actually use. Sites mix and adapt patterns, and the same site may present a different pattern in its phone and desktop views, so choosing representative patterns to compare requires a systematic survey and coding scheme rather than assuming that the three named styles map neatly onto practice. Third, speed is not only a matter of moving toward the target: a wrong-path click adds time both for the click itself and for the effort of noticing the error and returning to the right path, and this recovery cost is rarely measured directly. Separating it from forward progress requires event-level logging that defines when an error occurs and when the user is back on a correct path.

The problem is also important. Time lost in navigation is a cost to every user of a public service~~.~~ Evidence that a given pattern reduces errors or speeds recovery would give public-sector designers actionable guidance.

We therefore ask: **how do different nested navigation design patterns affect the speed at which users find a specific item?** We break this into four research questions:

* **RQ1.** What nested navigation design patterns are commonly used on Philippine government websites?

* **RQ2.** How do navigation styles vary across Philippine government websites?

* **RQ3.** How does the style of nested navigation impact the time spent recovering from a wrong-path click or error?

* **RQ4.** How do different navigation styles affect users’ item-finding speed on a Philippine government website?

RQ1 and RQ2 are descriptive and are addressed by the survey of Philippine government websites in (Phase 1). RQ3 and RQ4 are addressed empirically through an in-person, within-subjects usability test (Phase 3\) in which the independent variable is the navigation pattern (deep hierarchical, mega-menu, or nested dropdown) and the dependent variables are item-finding time, error count, and recovery time.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the notation and definitions we use. Section 4 details the methodology, including the analysis plan. Section 5 describes immediate next steps. Appendices provide the coding scheme, logging fields, and the test script.

# **2  Related Work**

## **2.1  Navigation Design and Website Usability**

Existing research on website navigation has examined the relationship between navigation design and website usability. In 2016, Pernice and Budiu \[4\] conducted a quantitative study involving 179 participants across six websites. They found that hidden navigation was used less frequently on desktops and resulted in task completion times that were at least 39% longer than with visible or combined navigation. Beyond navigation visibility, another factor that influences how users interact with a website is the organization of the navigation options and how they are presented within menus. Nielsen \[3\] reported findings from usability studies on the USA.gov website, which showed that users generally navigated quickly and successfully through mega-menus, although some users overlooked menu images or failed to recognize them as clickable elements. Going further to studying website usability of government websites, Verkijika and De Wet \[8\] evaluated 279 websites across 31 countries and identified the differences in website usability and organization across national contexts. These studies show the importance of navigation visibility, menu presentation, and website organization in the overall usability of a website. However, these studies only focused on the said areas and did not directly compare the effectiveness of the different nested navigation structures.

## **2.2  Hierarchical Menu Structure and Performance**

Hierarchical menu structures allow users to move from general to specific categories through navigation options organized into multiple levels. Previous research has studied how the depth, breadth, and organization of these menus affect the users’ ability to locate and select information. Hochheiser and Lazar \[1\] found that broader, shallower menu structures outperformed narrower, deeper hierarchies for screen reader users, with task completion time correlated with measures of navigation difficulty. Le et al. \[2\] reached a similar conclusion for health applications using tree testing, measuring task completion time, accuracy, and navigation paths. Extending this work in immersive augmented reality environments, Pourmemar et al. \[5\] study hierarchical drop-down menus in immersive AR, generating menus with varied depth and content from a lexical database and modeling pointing time and consumed endurance. Together, these works establish that structure (breadth, depth, and organization) affects performance and that time and path-based measures are workable, building on foundational work by Billingsley \[7\] on menu navigation structures. Meanwhile, in government information systems, Sheoran et al. \[9\] studied government portals internationally, including the usability characteristics that are related to the organization and retrieval of information of 75 countries' open government data portals. The big cross-country sample allows for the analysis of navigation patterns of government sites, though the study focuses on the analysis of the current portals and not on an experiment comparing different navigation structures. These studies collectively emphasize the importance of menu organization and information structure in supporting effective information retrieval. However, their approaches range from evaluating information architecture and accessibility to modeling cognitive effort and assessing existing government portals, rather than directly comparing the effects of different navigation patterns on users' task completion time, errors, and recovery time.

## **2.3  Navigation Difficulty and Backtracking**

Navigation difficulty and backtracking are also important indicators of how users interact with information structures and recover from unsuccessful navigation attempts. Thomas \[6\] investigated navigation difficulty using page-view data from a government website, examining browsing sequences and behaviors such as returning to previous pages as indicators of difficulty. On the other hand, van Oostendorp and Aggarwal \[10\] studied web navigation processes, highlighting navigation paths and backtracking as important aspects of users’ interaction with information structures. Although these studies differ in context, both demonstrate the value of analyzing navigation paths and backtracking to understand navigation difficulties and user recovery.

## **2.4  Gap and Implications for Design**

The literature covers hidden versus visible navigation \[4\], a mega-menu case on a government site \[3\], menu structure effects \[1, 2, 5\], and backtracking as a difficulty signal \[6, 10\]. In the literature we reviewed, we found no study that directly compares deep hierarchical, mega-menu, and nested dropdown navigation on government sites while measuring item-finding time, errors, and recovery time together. This gap motivates the three-phase methodology below: a survey of patterns in use on Philippine government websites, followed by prototype development and a task-based test that logs full navigation paths.

# **3  Preliminaries**

## **3.1  Navigation Patterns**

**Deep hierarchical navigation.** One level is visible at a time. Selecting an item replaces the current list with its children, through a page load or a single-panel drill-down, and a Back control returns to the parent level. The hierarchy has many levels (≥ 3\) \[12\].

![][image1]

*Image 1: Example of deep hierarchical navigation — landing page of Fiverr.*

![][image2]

*Image 2: Page loaded upon selecting “Programming & Tech” from Image 1\.*

![][image3]

*Image 3: Page loaded upon selecting “Python Developers” from Image 2\.*

**Mega-menu navigation.** Opening a top-level item displays a large panel that shows several levels at once, typically group headings with their links beneath them, possibly with images \[11\].

![][image4]

*Image 4: Example of a mega-menu — panel shown upon selecting “iPhone” from the Apple website.*

**Nested dropdown navigation.** Opening an item displays a list of its children while the parent list stays visible. Items that have children open further lists beside or beneath their parent, so the menu cascades one level at a time \[12\].

![][image5]

*Image 5: Example of a nested dropdown multilevel dropdown navigation from UXPin.*

Because the usability test runs on a phone, Section 4.3 states how each pattern is implemented for touch, without hover.

## **3.2  Navigation as a Tree**

We model a site’s navigation as a rooted tree *T* \= (*V*, *E*). A target item corresponds to a leaf *t*, and the *correct path* is *P*∗ \= (*v*0, *v*1, …, *v*k \= *t*) from the root to *t*, where *k* is the target’s depth. In the prototypes, each target appears at exactly one position in *T*, so *P*∗ is unique.

A *selection* is a tap on a menu item that is a node of *T*, whether the item opens its children (a branch) or opens a page (a leaf). Opening or closing the menu itself, and tapping a Back or collapse control, are *navigation actions*: they are logged but are not selections. At any moment the interface has a *current node* *c*, the node whose children or page are displayed (the root when only the top-level menu is shown). The participant is *on path* when *c* is a node of *P*∗. A selection is an *error* if it chooses a node that is not on *P*∗. The error count *E* is the number of such selections in a trial. A participant’s *trace* is the time-stamped sequence of selections and navigation actions.

## **3.3  Time Decomposition**

An *error episode* *j* begins at the time *s*j of an incorrect selection and ends at the time *e*j when the current node next returns to a node of *P*∗, either by selecting an on-path node or by a Back or collapse action that lands on an on-path node. If the trial ends (give-up or time-out) while an episode is open, *e*j is the trial end time. Recovery time and item-finding time are then

*R* \= Σj (*e*j − *s*j)     (1)

*T*find \= *T*clean \+ *R*     (2)

where *T*find is measured from the participant’s tap on Start to the selection of the target item, and *T*clean is the remaining time spent scanning the interface and making correct selections. For a trial with *E* \= 0, *R* \= 0, and *T*find \= *T*clean. Recovery time is analyzed on trials with *E* ≥ 1 (Section 4.7). Equation 2 lets us ask whether differences in *T*find across patterns come mainly from recovery or from slower correct navigation.

# **4  Methodology**

## **4.1  Overview and Hypotheses**

The study investigates how navigation patterns affect users’ item-finding behavior on Philippine government websites. Phase 1 surveys Philippine government websites to catalogue their navigation patterns (RQ1, RQ2) and selects one as the reference website. Phase 2 builds three (3) low-fidelity prototypes of that website, one per navigation pattern, each with an automated timer and event logger. Phase 3 tests the prototypes in person, with a within-subjects design, on a phone supplied by the researchers. All three prototypes use the same content tree, menu labels, target pages, visual styling, and page structure, and differ only in how the tree is presented, so that differences in performance can be attributed to the navigation pattern rather than to the content.

We examine three dependent variables: item-finding time, error count, and recovery time. In line with this, this study proposes the following null hypotheses:

* **H1:** There is no significant difference in item-finding time across the three (3) navigation patterns.

* **H2:** There is no significant difference in error count across the three (3) navigation patterns.

* **H3:** There is no significant difference in recovery time across the three (3) navigation patterns.

The corresponding alternative hypotheses (H1a–H3a) state that at least one pattern differs from the others. They are non-directional because the literature does not support a strong prediction about which nested style is fastest. RQ1 and RQ2 are descriptive and have no hypotheses. We also report secondary outcomes without formal hypotheses: task success, clean navigation time *T*clean, perceived difficulty, and pattern preference.

## **4.2  Phase 1: Survey and Reference Website Selection**

*Survey.* We will compile a list of Philippine national government websites, open each in a phone-width and a desktop-width browser view, and code its main navigation using the scheme in Appendix A. Two researchers code every site independently; disagreements are resolved by discussion. The output is the frequency of each pattern (RQ1) and how patterns vary by type of agency and by view (RQ2).

*Reference website selection.* The study will select one (1) commonly used Philippine government portal as the reference for developing the experimental low-fidelity prototypes. The selected website should contain a sufficiently broad range of services, information categories, forms, and nested menus to support realistic item-finding tasks, with target pages at depth three (3). The selection will be based on the website’s accessibility, relevance to the study’s intended users, and suitability for representing a typical government information system.

*Inclusion criteria.* A candidate is retained only if it meets all of the following:

1. It is an official, publicly accessible portal of the Philippine national government.

2. It organizes services or information through nested navigation.

3. Its content is in English or Filipino.

4. It works in a mobile browser.

5. It is actively maintained, with working links and current content.

*Ranking criteria.* Sites that meet all inclusion criteria are ranked to leave a single reference website. Two researchers score each site independently on the five criteria in Table 1, each from 0 to 4, and resolve differences by discussion. The weighted score is the sum of weight × score and ranges from 0 to 4\. The highest-scoring site becomes the reference website; ties are broken by the higher score on R1, then R2 to R5, and then by a random draw. The weights and anchors are fixed before any site is scored.

| Criterion | Weight | Score anchors (0 to 4\) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| R1  Task coverage: how many of the six test tasks (Appendix C) have a matching page at depth 3 or deeper | 30% | 0 to 1 tasks \= 0; 2 \= 1; 3 to 4 \= 2; 5 \= 3; all 6 \= 4 |
| R2  Nesting depth: menu levels in the main navigation, phone view | 25% | 1 level \= 0; 2 \= 1; 3 \= 3; 4 or more \= 4 |
| R3  Content breadth: top-level items in the main menu | 20% | 3 or fewer \= 0; 4 to 5 \= 1; 6 to 7 \= 2; 8 to 9 \= 3; 10 or more \= 4 |
| R4  Relevance to users: audience and purpose of the site | 15% | Mainly business or internal \= 0; general public, information only \= 2; general public, with services \= 4 |
| R5  Mobile usability and upkeep: menu works on a phone; share of 20 sampled links that work | 10% | Menu fails on a phone \= 0; under 80% of links work \= 1; 80 to 89% \= 2; 90 to 99% \= 3; 100% \= 4 |

*Table 1: Ranking criteria, weights, and score anchors.*

![][image6]

*Diagram 1: Website Selection Flowchart*

## **4.3  Phase 2: Prototype Development**

*Shared content tree.* The reference website’s navigation is simplified into one tree *T* used by all three prototypes. It has three levels of menu items below the root: level 1 (L1) categories, level 2 (L2) subcategories, and level 3 (L3) pages, so every target is a leaf at depth *k* \= 3\. Labels are copied from the reference website. The number of L1 categories and of items per level is fixed from the reference website after selection and is identical across patterns. Each target appears at one position only. The prototypes contain no search box, breadcrumbs, or cross-links; the logo returns to the start state, and the device’s system Back button is disabled, so the only way to move is through the menu.

*Pattern implementation for touch.* The test runs on a phone, so every pattern is tap-based, with no hover. Table 2 states how each pattern is implemented.

| Pattern | How a level opens | What stays visible | Selections needed |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Deep hierarchical | Tapping an item replaces the list in the same panel with its children (single-panel drill-down, no page load). A Back control at the top returns to the parent level. | Only the current level. | 3 (L1, L2, L3) |
| Mega-menu | Tapping an L1 item opens a full-width panel that shows all L2 group headings with their L3 links at once, in one scrollable panel. L2 headings are labels, and L3 links are selectable. | The L1 bar and the open panel (L2 and L3 together). | 2 (L1, L3) |
| Nested dropdown | Tapping an L1 item opens a list of its L2 items beneath it. Tapping an L2 item opens its L3 list beneath it, indented. Tapping an open item collapses it. | The parent lists stay visible while child lists open, one level at a time. | 3 (L1, L2, L3) |

*Table 2: Implementation of the three navigation patterns in the prototypes.*

The minimum number of selections differs by pattern (2 in the mega-menu, 3 in the others) because the mega-menu shows two levels at once. This difference is part of what the pattern is, so it is not removed. It is logged for every trial so that it can be reported alongside the results.

*Automated timer and logger.* Each prototype is a local web app (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) that runs in the browser of the supplied phone without a network connection. A researcher-only configuration screen, protected by a passcode, sets the participant ID, sequence, pattern, task, and target item before each task, so the target can be changed for the intended task without rebuilding the prototype. The participant sees a task screen with the scenario text and a Start button. The timer starts when the participant taps Start and stops when the target item is selected, after which the app shows a completion screen. Selecting any other L3 page opens a placeholder page that reads “This is not the page you were asked to find”, with a Back control, and counts as an error. A Give up button is always visible, and the app ends the task automatically at 180 seconds. Every tap and navigation action is logged with a timestamp (milliseconds since Start), the node ID, and an automatically computed on-path flag (Appendix B). The log is saved on the device and exported by the researcher after the session. *T*find, *E*, and *R* are computed from the log by a script.

*Fidelity.* The prototypes are low-fidelity: simplified visual design, the reference website’s labels, and static placeholder content on target pages. They are interactive enough for participants to move between menu levels, select items, and reach target pages.

*Task and target-item preparation.* The six experimental tasks are specified in Appendix C. They form three matched pairs (A, B, and C). Each target is an L3 page, no two targets share an L2 parent, and the task text describes a goal in everyday words without copying the target’s menu label or its parents’ labels. Pairs are matched on target depth, on the number of sibling items at the target’s level, and on label clarity, and the pilot checks that the pairs are similar in difficulty. A separate practice tree on a non-government topic (a public library) is used for practice tasks, so participants do not see experimental content before the timed tasks.

## **4.4  Phase 3: Usability Test**

*Design.* Within-subjects with one independent variable, navigation pattern, at three levels: deep hierarchical (DH), mega-menu (MM), and nested dropdown (ND). Each participant completes two (2) tasks per pattern (six in total). Participants are assigned in rotation to one of three sequences (Table 3). The sequences form a Latin square, so across sequences each pattern appears once in each block position and is paired once with each task pair. The order of the two tasks within a pair alternates between consecutive participants in the same sequence.

| Sequence | Block 1 | Block 2 | Block 3 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| S1 | DH with pair A (T1, T2) | MM with pair B (T3, T4) | ND with pair C (T5, T6) |
| S2 | MM with pair A (T1, T2) | ND with pair B (T3, T4) | DH with pair C (T5, T6) |
| S3 | ND with pair A (T1, T2) | DH with pair B (T3, T4) | MM with pair C (T5, T6) |

*Table 3: Counterbalancing of navigation pattern and task pair (3 × 3 Latin square).*

*Participants and recruitment.* We plan for N \= 15 adult participants who use the web regularly, ten (10) per sequence. This sample size is provisional and will be confirmed by a power analysis after the pilot testing, rounded up to a multiple of three so that the sequences stay balanced. Basic demographics, self-reported familiarity with government websites, and prior use of the reference website will be collected. Ethics approval and informed consent are required before recruitment. Participants will be recruited online, specifically via Facebook and Messenger. The researchers will post a recruitment post on Facebook and send invitations through Messenger to friends and family members who may be qualified to participate. Interested participants will complete a short Google Form to check whether they meet the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and participation is voluntary and unpaid. Sessions are held in person in a quiet room.

**Inclusion criteria:**

1. Aged 18 and above.

2. Has visited at least one Philippine government website in the past 12 months (self-reported).

3. Uses websites at least once a week.

4. Uses a smartphone regularly.

5. Gives informed consent.

**Exclusion criteria:**

1. Relies on assistive technology (such as a screen reader or switch control) to use a phone, since the prototypes are not built or tested for it.

2. Works or studies in web design, UX, or software development, or has worked on a government website, since expertise may change how they read menus.

3. Cannot comfortably read the language of the prototype content (English or Filipino).

4. Has taken part in the pilot test or has seen the prototypes or task set before.

5. Is a member of the research team.

*Apparatus.* All sessions are run in person on a recorded model of smartphone supplied by the researchers. These same device models, screen size, operating system, browser, brightness, and portrait orientation are used in every session, with notifications turned off. The prototype runs locally with no network connection, so there is no loading delay. A researcher sits beside the participant to hand over the device and start each task from the configuration screen, but gives no hints. Think-aloud is not used during timed tasks, because it can alter task time.

*Recordings.* For each session we collect: (1) the automated event log, which is the primary data, (2) a screen recording of the supplied device as a backup for checking the log, and (3) the demographic questionnaire, the post-task difficulty ratings, and the final feedback questionnaire. Participants are referred to by ID only, and files are stored on Google Drive with access limited to the research team.

**4.5  Procedure**

The usability test will follow these steps and take about 30 minutes per participant with breaks (to be confirmed in the pilot):

1. **Consent and demographic questionnaire.** Participants will review the study information, provide informed consent, and complete a short demographic questionnaire.

2. **Briefing and practice.** The researcher reads the standard briefing (Appendix C) and shows the participant how to hold the device and where the Start and Give up buttons are. Participants will then complete a practice task using a separate prototype or interface not included in the actual experiment. This will familiarize them with the task format without exposing them to the experimental target items.

3. **Pattern blocks and experimental tasks.** Each participant will complete six (6) timed information-finding tasks: two (2) tasks for each of the three navigation patterns, in the block order given by their sequence (Table 3). For each experimental task, the researcher sets the participant ID, pattern, and target item on the configuration screen and hands over the device. The participant reads the scenario on the task screen and taps Start. The timer starts at that tap and stops automatically when the participant selects the target item. A task is classified as unsuccessful if the participant does not reach the target within three (3) minutes (the app ends the task automatically) or taps Give up. The six experimental tasks are listed in exact wording read to participants in Appendix C.

4. **Difficulty rating.** After each task, participants will be asked to provide a brief rating of perceived task difficulty on the device, using the Single Ease Question (7-point scale from 1, very difficult, to 7, very easy).

5. **Breaks.** A short break is offered between blocks.

6. **Final feedback and debriefing.** After all tasks have been completed, participants rank the three menu styles by preference, may add comments, and will receive a brief explanation of the study’s purpose and an opportunity to give additional feedback.

Diagram 2 shows every step of the experiment, from recruitment to analysis.

## **4.6  Measures**

**Dependent variables:** (1) *item-finding time*, the time to locate the requested item (*T*find); (2) *error count*, the number of incorrect navigation selections before reaching the target (*E*); and (3) *recovery time*, the time to return to the correct path after an incorrect selection (*R*), following the definitions in Section 3\. 

**Secondary outcomes:** task success, clean navigation time (*T*clean), perceived difficulty, and the preference ranking of the three patterns.

**Covariates:** the minimum number of selections for the pattern (2 or 3), block position, task pair, familiarity with government websites, and prior use of the reference website.

All timing and navigation measures are computed by a script from the automated log, using the tree to flag each selection as on or off the correct path. A researcher checks a random sample of trials against the screen recordings to confirm that the log matches what happened on screen.

## **4.7  Analysis Plan**

Each participant contributes six trials, so trials are nested within participants. Table 4 gives the planned primary analysis for each outcome.

| Outcome | Type | Primary analysis |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| *T*find (H1) | Continuous, right-skewed; log-transformed | Linear mixed model: pattern fixed effect; block position and task pair as covariates; participant random intercept |
| *E* (H2) | Count | Poisson or negative binomial mixed model with the same terms |
| *R* (H3) | Continuous, log-transformed; trials with *E* ≥ 1 only | Linear mixed model with the same terms; participants with no errors under a pattern contribute no *R* for that pattern |
| Success | Binary | Logistic mixed model |

*Table 4: Planned analyses.*

If the assumptions of a mixed model are not met, the fallback is a Friedman test on each participant’s values per pattern, with Wilcoxon signed-rank follow-ups.

H1 to H3 are each tested two-sided at α \= .05. If the omnibus pattern effect is significant, the three pairwise contrasts are tested with Holm correction. We report effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals: ratios of geometric means for times, rate ratios for counts, and odds ratios for success. *T*find, *E*, and *R* are analyzed on successful trials, and success rate is analyzed separately, with the number of unsuccessful trials reported by pattern. For descriptive summaries of unsuccessful trials, an open error episode ends at the trial end. No observation is removed by a statistical rule. A trial is excluded only if the log or screen recording shows a device or app fault, and this decision is made before looking at which pattern the trial belongs to. The pilot supplies the effect size and variance estimates for the power analysis that fixes the final sample size.

# **5  Future Work**

The next steps follow the order of the three phases. We will first compile the Philippine candidate government websites, code their navigation with the scheme in Appendix A, apply the inclusion criteria, and score the remaining candidates using the ranking criteria in Table 1\. We will then design and develop the three low-fidelity prototypes from the selected website, and prepare and validate the experimental tasks by mapping the six scenarios in Appendix C to real target pages. A pilot study will follow to test the tasks, the timing and recording procedure, and the logging fields, and its results will be used to run the power analysis that fixes the final sample size and the analysis plan. After obtaining ethical approval, we will recruit participants, conduct the experiment, analyze the logged data, and report the findings and their implications for the design of government websites.

# **Appendices**

## **A  Navigation Pattern Coding Scheme**

| Pattern | Coding cues |
| :---- | :---- |
| Deep hierarchical | Options revealed one level at a time through page loads or single-panel drill-down; many levels (≥ 3). |
| Mega-menu | Large panel opened from a top-level item showing multiple groups of links (possibly with images) at once. |
| Nested dropdown | Cascading list menus that open sub-menus beside or beneath the parent item. |
| Other | Patterns not fitting above (e.g., search-only, tiles); recorded with a note. |

*Table A1: Coding scheme for Phase 1\.*

## **B  Trial Logging Fields**

| Field | Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| participant\_id, trial\_id | Identifiers. |
| sequence, block\_position | Sequence (S1 to S3) and block position (1 to 3). |
| pattern, task\_id, task\_pair | Pattern (DH, MM, ND), task (T1 to T6 or practice), and pair (A to C). |
| target\_node | Target set on the configuration screen. |
| min\_selections | Minimum selections to reach the target in this pattern (2 or 3). |
| t\_start, t\_end, end\_reason | Task start and target-reached times (s), and why the task ended (target, give\_up, timeout). |
| selections\[\] | Time-stamped menu selections, each flagged on/off the correct path. |
| E | Number of off-path selections. |
| R | Sum of error-episode durations (s). |
| T\_find, T\_clean | Item-finding time and clean navigation time (s). |
| difficulty\_rating | Single Ease Question response (1 to 7). |
| success | Found target within time limit (Y/N). |

*Table B1: Fields recorded for each trial.*

## **C  Test Script**

**C.1  Researcher setup for each task.** Before handing over the device, the researcher opens the configuration screen, enters the participant ID and sequence, selects the pattern and task for the current block, confirms that the target item shown for the task is correct, and returns to the task screen. The device is handed over only when the task screen is showing.

**C.2  Briefing (read aloud).**

“Thank you for taking part. Today you will use a website on this phone to find pages about government services. We are testing the website’s menus, not you, and there are no right or wrong ways to look. For each task, you will see a short situation on the screen. Read it, then tap Start. A timer runs while you look for the page, so please work as you normally would. When you reach the right page, the screen will tell you the task is complete. If you open a page that is not the one you need, you can go back and keep looking. If you cannot find the page, you can tap Give up at any time. After each task, you will rate how difficult it was. Before each new type of menu, you will get one practice task. I cannot help during a task, but you can ask for a break between blocks. Do you have any questions?”

**C.3  Practice tasks.**

| Practice | Scenario shown on the task screen |
| :---- | :---- |
| P1 | You want to read a book on your phone. Find the page that explains how to borrow an e-book. |
| P2 | Your library card has expired. Find the page that explains how to renew it. |
| P3 | You and your classmates need a quiet place to work. Find the page that explains how to book a study room. |

*Table C1: Practice tasks. Practice tasks use the pattern of the block they precede.*

**C.4  Experimental tasks (scenario text shown on the task screen).**

| Task | Pair | Scenario shown to the participant | Target page (L1 › L2 › L3) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| T1 | A | You want to travel abroad and have never had a passport. Find the page that explains how to apply for one. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |
| T2 | A | Your driver’s license will expire next month. Find the page that explains how to renew it. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |
| T3 | B | You need an official copy of your birth certificate for a school requirement. Find the page that explains how to request one. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |
| T4 | B | You are opening a small online shop and want to register its business name. Find the page that explains how to register one. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |
| T5 | C | You just started your first job, and your employer asks for your Tax Identification Number. Find the page that explains how to apply for one. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |
| T6 | C | You have started working and need a Social Security System number. Find the page that explains how to apply for one. | \[to be mapped from the reference website\] |

*Table C2: Experimental task script. Scenario wording is checked against the final menu labels so that it does not copy a target’s label or its parents’ labels.*

The six tasks span services run by different agencies, so a single agency website is unlikely to hold all of them. R1 in Table 1 therefore favours a portal that links to services across agencies; if no candidate covers all six, the tasks are re-mapped to the services the selected site does cover, keeping the three matched pairs.

**C.5  Rules during tasks.** The researcher does not give hints or confirm whether the participant is on the right path. If the participant asks for help, the researcher says: “Please do whatever you would normally do.” If the participant gets stuck, the participant may tap Give up. If the device or app fails during a task, the researcher records the fault, and the trial is handled as described in Section 4.7.

**C.6  Debriefing (read aloud).** “That was the last task. Please rank the three menu styles you used from the one you liked most to the one you liked least, and add any comments. The study compares how quickly people find pages with different menu styles on government websites. Thank you for your time.”
